Catalytic Electrophilic Thiocarbocyclization of Allenes
Quanbin Jiang, † Huimin Li, † and Xiaodan Zhao *
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2021, 23, 8777 −8782 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: An e ﬃcient approach via catalytic electrophilic
thiocarbocyclization of allenes to construct indene-based sul ﬁdes
with excellent regioselectivities is disclosed. The reactions were
carried out at low temperatures by selenide catalysis in the presence
of TMSOTf. Not only electrophilic arylthio reagents but also
electrophilic alkylthio reagents worked well under these conditions.
Furthermore, the method could be applied to intermolecular azidothiolation of allenes.
S
ulfur-containing compounds make up an important class of
compounds. Their structural motifs are found in a wide
range of biologically active molecules and drugs. 1,2 They can
serve as building blocks for the synthesis of valuable
compounds and also act as ligands and organocatalysts in
organic reactions.
3,4 Due to their importance, numerous
methods have been developed to construct these compounds
via metal catalysis and organocatalysis in the past several
decades.
5,6 For example, transition metal-catalyzed cross-
coupling of alkenyl halides with sulfur compounds as well as
catalytic hydrothiolation of alkynes to synthesize alkenyl
sulﬁdes has been demonstrated.
7 In particular, as a facile
route, catalytic electrophilic thiolation of unsaturated hydro-
carbon compounds to construct sul ﬁdes has attracted a great
deal of attention. 5b,8−13 This kind of reaction can be carried
out under mild and metal-free conditions. When utilizing
electrophilic sulfur reagents, the reactions generally go through
a thiiranium or thiirenium ion intermediate, followed by attack
of the nucleophiles to give the ﬁnal sul ﬁde products, which
oﬀers a convenient method for quickly constructing multi-
functionalized sulfur compounds. In this scenario, the
thiolation of alkenes and alkynes has been studied ( Scheme
1, top).
8−12 In contrast, the thiolation of allenes, unsaturated
compounds with unique structural features, including
orthogonal π-orbitals composed of sp 2 and sp carbons, has
been rarely investigated ( Scheme 1, bottom).13 To the best of
our knowledge, only oxy- and halothiolation of allenes have
been demonstrated.
With their unique features, allenes are usually very reactive
and can be converted into a variety of products by reacting
with di ﬀerent compounds.
14,15 Unlike the electrophilic
thiolation of alkenes and alkynes, electrophilic thiolation of
allenes might be more challenging for following three reasons.
(i) Highly reactive allenes easily decompose under reaction
conditions. (ii) Allenes contain two double bonds, resulting in
the issue of site selectivity on the three carbons. (iii) The
properties of a possible intermediate, thiiranium ion with a
vinyl carbon, remain elusive. In spite of the challenges, we
discovered that allenes could undergo electrophilic thiocarbo-
cyclization to give sul ﬁdes with high regioselectivities by
selenide catalysis in the presence of a Lewis acid. Herein, we
report the ﬁndings.
The Lewis basic selenium-catalyzed electrophilic reaction
has emerged as an intriguing strategy for the synthesis of
various valuable molecules.
8−10,16,17 In this reaction, Lewis
basic selenium compounds can activate electrophilic halogen
or sulfur reagents to form a selenium-captured cation ion
intermediate. The intermediate has a proper reactivity and can
lead to less side products compared with the solo electrophile
E
+ ion. This advantage leads to Lewis basic selenium catalysis
having good applications in electrophilic halogenation and
thiolation of alkenes, alkynes, and even arenes. Our group has
been working on organoselenium catalysis. We have developed
Lewis basic selenium-catalyzed electrophilic tri ﬂuoromethylth-

alkenes.10a,c−e Additionally, catalytic electrophilic thiolation
of alkynes has been investigated. 10b As a continuation of our
interest, we attempted to extend Lewis basic selenium catalysis
to electrophilic thiolation of highly reactive substrates, allenes.
By electrophilic reaction, introducing a long-chain alkylthio
group into the parent molecules is more di ﬃcult than
introducing an arylthio group because of the lower reactivity
of electrophilic long-chain alkylthio reagents. To challenge this,
we initiated our thiolation study with racemic diphenyl allene
1a as a model substrate and an electrophilic alkylthiolating
reagent, 1-(propylthio)pyrrolidine-2,5-dione ( 2a), as another
component. A thiocyclized compound based on a useful
indene sca ﬀold was expected as the desired product in the
presence of a catalytic amount of selenide ( Table 1). When the
reaction was carried out at room temperature using diphenyl
selenide as a catalyst and TMSOTf as an additive, no desired
product was observed at all (entry 1). Considering the high
reactivity of allene 1a, decreasing the reaction temperature
might bene ﬁt the reaction. When the reaction was performed
at 0 °C, gratifyingly, the desired product was formed in
excellent regioselectivity, albeit in low yield (entry 2). Further
decreasing the reaction temperature led to higher yields
(entries 3 and 4). The reaction gave the best yield at −60 °C
(entries 4 and 5). When the reaction time was prolonged to 22
h, the desired product was a ﬀorded in 85% isolated yield
(entry 6). Other additives such as Lewis acids TESOTf and
BF
3·OEt2 and Brønsted acids TfOH and Tf 2NH were less
eﬀective, leading to lower yields (entries 7 −10, respectively).
When the amount of additive was reduced to 0.5 equiv or
increased to 2 equiv, the products were formed in lower yields
(entries 11 and 12). Furthermore, the e ﬀect of di ﬀerent
chalcogenide catalysts was studied. When using the selenide
catalysts bearing electron-withdrawing or electron-donating
groups on the phenyl ring, the reactions gave lower yields
(entries 13 −15). Other chalcogenides such as PhSPh, Ph
3P
S, and Ph 3PSe had weaker e ﬀects on the reaction (entries
16−18, respectively). Possibly, PhSePh provides the optimal
Lewis basicity. It is noted that the absence of a Lewis acid
resulted in no reaction; however, without a selenide catalyst,
the reaction gave the desired product in 61% yield (entries 19
and 20). These results revealed that the Lewis acid plays a
signiﬁcant role in this transformation and the background
reaction is strong without selenide.
With the optimal conditions in hand, we ﬁrst evaluated the
scope of electrophilic sulfur reagents ( Scheme 2 ). When the
alkyl-chain length on the electrophilic alkylthiolating reagents
was adjusted, the reactions still proceeded e ﬃciently to give
the corresponding products in high yields ( 3b, 83%; 3c, 79%).
Moreover, a benzyl electrophilic sulfur reagent or an
alkylthiolating reagent with a halo substituent such as Cl-
still aﬀorded the desired products in good yields ( 3d, 75%; 3e,
83%). Importantly, the method was also suitable for other
electrophilic sulfur reagents. Using a more reactive electro-
philic tri ﬂuoromethylthiolating reagent, the reaction gave the
triﬂuoromethylthio product 3f, a class of useful compounds,
18
in 79% yield. When arylthiolating reagents were utilized,
similarly, the reactions worked well to give the desired
products in good yields ( 3g−3i,7 3 −83%). Even if a sterically
hindered o-methyl-substituted sulfur reagent was used, the
desired product 3j was formed in good yield. These results
indicated that the method is general.
Next, the scope of allene substrates were evaluated ( Scheme
3). The e ﬀect of di ﬀerent substituents on the allene substrates
was investigated. When R 1 was a methyl group and R 2 was an

group of R 2 had an impact on the reactions. Electron-donating
groups resulted in relatively lower yields than electron-
withdrawing ones ( 3k−3o,6 4 −83%). It is noted that when
the substituent, e.g., MeO-, was placed at the ortho position of
the phenyl group, the reaction was slightly a ﬀected, still giving
the desired product 3p in good yield. For the aryl nucleophile,
the substituents on it had a similar electronic e ﬀect compared
with the e ﬀect of those on the phenyl group of R
2. Electron-
donating groups usually led to yields that were relatively lower
than those of electron-withdrawing ones except the -CN group
(3q−3u,6 8−86%). Possibly, the -CN group was too electron-
withdrawing, so that the corresponding allene was more highly
reactive, increasing the likelihood of side reactions. When R
1
was an aryl group and R 2 was an aryl or alkyl group, the
reactions still proceeded smoothly to a ﬀord the desired
products in good yields ( 3v, 61%; 3w, 67%). Furthermore,
the R1 group could be a long-chain alkyl group. To more easily
purify the desired products, an electrophilic arylthiolating
reagent was used ( 3x, 99%; 3y, 60%). Interestingly, when
allene 1q with a methoxy group at the meta position was
utilized as the substrate, the reaction gave product 3z in good
yield, in which the electron-rich aryl group acted as a
nucleophile ( eq 1 ). As depicted in transition states TS-1 and
TS-2, the methoxy substituent can cause the phenyl group to
be more electron-rich. Subsequently, the electron-rich aryl
group is preferred as a nucleophile to the phenyl group even in

To further explore the e ﬃciency, practicality, and generality
of this method, relevant studies were conducted. First, a gram-
scale experiment was performed. When 1a (5.0 mmol) was
treated with electrophilic sulfur reagent under similar
conditions, product 3a was still obtained in high yield (eq
2). Then, an intermolecular azidothiolation reaction with 1r as
the substrate was tested under similar conditions (eq 3). The
desired product was formed with high regioselectivity in
moderate yield along with the formation of a thiocarbocycliza-
tion byproduct. This preliminary result re ﬂected the possibility
of intermolecular reaction. Finally, the kinetic resolution of this
kind of reaction was investigated, although the background

with sulfur reagent 2i in the presence of chiral bifunctional
selenide catalyst C5, cyclized product 3aa could be formed, but
without ee. Similarly, the other catalysts such as selenide C6
and sul ﬁde C7 delivered no enantioselectivity. Even if the
reaction of 1f ran for 1 h, 3aa was also formed in 40% yield
without ee. The results revealed that the current conditions are
not e ﬀective for the resolution of racemic allenes.
On the basis of the results presented above and previous
studies,
10a a possible mechanism is proposed in Scheme 4 .A n
electrophilic sulfur reagent is ﬁrst activated by the PhSePh
catalyst with the assistance of Lewis acid TMSOTf via
transition state I. A selenide-captured sulfonium ion inter-
mediate II is formed. Then, reaction of II with substrates gives
cyclic thiiranium ion intermediate III with high regioselectivity.
Subsequent nucleophilic attack of the aromatic ring on the
thiiranium ion unit a ﬀords the desired products 3 and
regenerates the selenide catalyst. However, the properties of
the cyclic thiiranium ion with a vinyl cabon are unknown. The
thiiranium ion might be very unstable to decomposition to the
corresponding carbon cation and then undergo nucleophilic
attack to give the ﬁnal products. This could be one of the
potential reasons why the kinetic resolution of the reaction
does not work. Presumably, the thiiranium ion intermediate,
e.g., IV, formed from the other double bond on the allene
substrate might be more stable. Due to the steric hindrance
that disfavors the formation of the quaternary carbon center,
the subsequent cyclization may not proceed easily. Only in the
case of 3z does the strong nucleophilicity of the electron-rich
aryl group overcome the steric hindrance to furnish product
3z. There might be an equilibrium between intermediates IV
and III, leading to products 3.
In summary, we have developed an e ﬃcient method for the
synthesis of indene-based sul ﬁdes with high regioselectivities in
good yields via organoselenium-catalyzed electrophilic thio-
carbocyclization of allenes. This method could be applied to a
similar intermolecular reaction. It is noted that the reaction
temperature is crucial in the reactions. This is the ﬁrst example
of Lewis basic chalcogenide-catalyzed reaction of allenes.
Further investigations of chalcogenide-catalyzed reactions are
ongoing in our laboratory.

Catalytic Electrophilic Thiocarbocyclization of Allenes
Quanbin Jiang, † Huimin Li, † and Xiaodan Zhao *

ABSTRACT: An e ﬃcient approach via catalytic electrophilic
thiocarbocyclization of allenes to construct indene-based sul ﬁdes
with excellent regioselectivities is disclosed. The reactions were
carried out at low temperatures by selenide catalysis in the presence
of TMSOTf. Not only electrophilic arylthio reagents but also
electrophilic alkylthio reagents worked well under these conditions.
Furthermore, the method could be applied to intermolecular azidothiolation of allenes.
S
ulfur-containing compounds make up an important class of
compounds. Their structural motifs are found in a wide
range of biologically active molecules and drugs. 1,2 They can
serve as building blocks for the synthesis of valuable
compounds and also act as ligands and organocatalysts in
organic reactions.
3,4 Due to their importance, numerous
methods have been developed to construct these compounds
via metal catalysis and organocatalysis in the past several
decades.
5,6 For example, transition metal-catalyzed cross-
coupling of alkenyl halides with sulfur compounds as well as
catalytic hydrothiolation of alkynes to synthesize alkenyl
sulﬁdes has been demonstrated.
7 In particular, as a facile
route, catalytic electrophilic thiolation of unsaturated hydro-
carbon compounds to construct sul ﬁdes has attracted a great
deal of attention. 5b,8−13 This kind of reaction can be carried
out under mild and metal-free conditions. When utilizing
electrophilic sulfur reagents, the reactions generally go through
a thiiranium or thiirenium ion intermediate, followed by attack
of the nucleophiles to give the ﬁnal sul ﬁde products, which
oﬀers a convenient method for quickly constructing multi-
functionalized sulfur compounds. In this scenario, the
thiolation of alkenes and alkynes has been studied ( Scheme
1, top).
8−12 In contrast, the thiolation of allenes, unsaturated
compounds with unique structural features, including
orthogonal π-orbitals composed of sp 2 and sp carbons, has
been rarely investigated ( Scheme 1, bottom).13 To the best of
our knowledge, only oxy- and halothiolation of allenes have
been demonstrated.
With their unique features, allenes are usually very reactive
and can be converted into a variety of products by reacting
with di ﬀerent compounds.
14,15 Unlike the electrophilic
thiolation of alkenes and alkynes, electrophilic thiolation of
allenes might be more challenging for following three reasons.
(i) Highly reactive allenes easily decompose under reaction
conditions. (ii) Allenes contain two double bonds, resulting in
the issue of site selectivity on the three carbons. (iii) The
properties of a possible intermediate, thiiranium ion with a
vinyl carbon, remain elusive. In spite of the challenges, we
discovered that allenes could undergo electrophilic thiocarbo-
cyclization to give sul ﬁdes with high regioselectivities by
selenide catalysis in the presence of a Lewis acid. Herein, we
report the ﬁndings.
The Lewis basic selenium-catalyzed electrophilic reaction
has emerged as an intriguing strategy for the synthesis of
various valuable molecules.
8−10,16,17 In this reaction, Lewis
basic selenium compounds can activate electrophilic halogen
or sulfur reagents to form a selenium-captured cation ion
intermediate. The intermediate has a proper reactivity and can
lead to less side products compared with the solo electrophile
E
+ ion. This advantage leads to Lewis basic selenium catalysis
having good applications in electrophilic halogenation and
thiolation of alkenes, alkynes, and even arenes. Our group has
been working on organoselenium catalysis. We have developed
Lewis basic selenium-catalyzed electrophilic tri ﬂuoromethylth-

10a a possible mechanism is proposed in Scheme 4 .A n
electrophilic sulfur reagent is ﬁrst activated by the PhSePh
catalyst with the assistance of Lewis acid TMSOTf via
transition state I. A selenide-captured sulfonium ion inter-
mediate II is formed. Then, reaction of II with substrates gives
cyclic thiiranium ion intermediate III with high regioselectivity.
Subsequent nucleophilic attack of the aromatic ring on the
thiiranium ion unit a ﬀords the desired products 3 and
regenerates the selenide catalyst. However, the properties of
the cyclic thiiranium ion with a vinyl cabon are unknown. The
thiiranium ion might be very unstable to decomposition to the
corresponding carbon cation and then undergo nucleophilic
attack to give the ﬁnal products. This could be one of the
potential reasons why the kinetic resolution of the reaction
does not work. Presumably, the thiiranium ion intermediate,
e.g., IV, formed from the other double bond on the allene
substrate might be more stable. Due to the steric hindrance
that disfavors the formation of the quaternary carbon center,
the subsequent cyclization may not proceed easily. Only in the
case of 3z does the strong nucleophilicity of the electron-rich
aryl group overcome the steric hindrance to furnish product
3z. There might be an equilibrium between intermediates IV
and III, leading to products 3.
In summary, we have developed an e ﬃcient method for the
synthesis of indene-based sul ﬁdes with high regioselectivities in
good yields via organoselenium-catalyzed electrophilic thio-
carbocyclization of allenes. This method could be applied to a
similar intermolecular reaction. It is noted that the reaction
temperature is crucial in the reactions. This is the ﬁrst example
of Lewis basic chalcogenide-catalyzed reaction of allenes.
Further investigations of chalcogenide-catalyzed reactions are
ongoing in our laboratory.
